In the year 2000s, a new illegal activity termed ‘tax asset stripping,’ where people bought, then quickly sold inactive companies to steal their assets including funds meant for taxes, emerged and was prosecuted. In 1994, Henrik Hasslund, a Danish national, became aware via media of an investigation on him. He cooperated with law enforcements throughout 1995. In September of '95 Hasslund got arrested; he remained in custody until December 22 of the year.

A lengthy trial commenced from '1996 through 2001, featuring Hasslund among several others. Hasslund was found guilty for his participation in the 'tax asset stripping,' a charge that led to both jail time, forfeiture, and prohibition from engaging in certain businesses for an indeterminate timeframe. Hasslund disputed the proceedings' duration, arguing it violated legal human rights standards. However, courts argued the complexity and scale of the crime warranted extended investigations and trials.

Appeals processes continued from 2001 onwards, leading to further delays and postponements. In October 2004, Hasslund and his co-defendants were again rejected permission to appeal further to the Supreme Court. The case demonstrated profound legal challenges and the intricate nature of prosecuting complex economic crimes.
0.75.1:
The case started as an application by Mr D. Stępniak, born in the year 1964 living now at Bytom against Republic Poland on July 21th 14 years ago, filed with the Court under the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government was represented by Mr J. Wołąsiewicz who works at their foreign ministry. On Jan 25th four years prior the President of section decided to notify Poland regarding Mr Stępniak’s application. The examination of the merits was decided together during the application's admissibility phase following provisions outlined at Article 29 section three.

In the case details, Mr Stępniak got captured on Oct 21st of this year. Following his arrest, District Court Wodzisław Śląski ruled him to be detained on allegations of organized crime. The court made their decision based reports and findings suggesting Stępniak was involved and guilty. His appeal failed and later court orders extended his detention multiple times until different dates including Oct 8, 2003, Jan 22, and July 22 of subsequent years. Reasons cited included preventing interference in ongoing investigations and obtaining substantial evidence. Also mentioned his past criminal activities. Throughout a period of detention, Stępniak met his wife a few times like around Dec 11 and Nov 18, this year.

On Sep 22nd, a charge of fraud was officially recorded against Mr Stępniak. Trial sessions occurred on Jan, Feb, then Oct 26 last year. In conclusion, he was found guilty of all charges. Notably, some of his letters sent in the period of Jan to Mar last year were censored by Wodzisław Śląski District Court.
0.75.2: The case started in an application (number not provided) by Turkish national Mr Nusret Amutgan against Turkey submitted on 29 December 2003 following the Convention for protecting Human rights ("Convention"). The applicant’s case was represented in Gaziantep by Ms B Özpolat and the Turkish government represented by their agent responded in this matter. On the declaration on 04 January, 2008, by the court, only a part was admissible and asked the government for communication concerning inadequate legal assistance during police custody. The court also decided on the merits at one go. Facts of the case were as follows- the applicant born year unknown, currently in prison in Gaziantep, was arrested during military activity of armed forces on 27th April in 1998 on suspicion of PKK membership. The applicant was detained at a gendarme station without access of lawyer and his confession was recorded. In his statement, he claimed joining PKK as early as Feburary, and participation multiple armed activities from then. On May, 1998, he stood in front of public prosecutor and judge again without a lawyer confirming his past actions and statements. He remained in custody on order of the judge. On Wednesday 05, 1998, at Diyarbakir State Security Court, the public prosecutor filed charges against the applicant for attempting territorial secession. They asked for death penalty under Criminal Code Clause. Trial started in August of '98, applicant represented through his lawyer. He confessed joining PKK earlier and receiving military training. He admitted some crimes. He also told the court that he was forced to sign his statement at the gendarmerie station. In Nov '02, Diyarbakir State Security Court convicted the applicant and imposed death penalty, which got reduced. The court concluded that the applicant had committed several unlawful acts based his statements post-arrest admission, and his testimony throughout trial, involving killings and kidnappings. His appeal was rejected in September of '03, by the Court of Cassation.
0.75.3:
The case began from two applications filed (nos. unspecified) before the European Commission of Human Rights against Republic of Turkey by two Turkish citizens—Mr. Mustafa Sarı (born in '73 living in Ankara at time) and Ms. Sibel Çolak (born 77, also from Ankara) on March fourth, '98, utilizing the former Article of the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention"). The applicants were provided with legal assistance and were represented by Mrs. E. Çıtak; a lawyer from Istanbul. The Government did not appoint any representative.

On the first of Feb., '00, the First Section of the Court decided to combine the applications and declared them partly inadmissible while notifying the Government of the complaints under Article five sections ones & threes and Article eight. The court's Sectional compositions were altered in Novembers '01 & four by Rule 25 section 1 of their Rules. This case then moved to a restructured Second Section according to Rule five-two section 1.

Subsequently, the applicants and governmenet each submitted their views on both parties' observations per Rule fifty-nine section first. They exchanged replies. Adhering to Article twenty-nine section 3, the court decided on the admissibility of the cases simultaneously as they moved into the merit phase. The facts of this case involve two individuals named Mr Mustafa Sarı, and Ms. Sibel Çolak, detained due to a probe involving THKP-C Dev Yol – Devrim Hareketi (Turkish People's Liberation Party-Front – Revolutionary Way – Revolutionary Movement).

On the seventeenth, November '97 around midnight, they apprehended the applicants at Ankara's security police station. Their detention was extended, under section sixteen of Law number 2845, for initial duration up till November 21st, '97, granted by a public prosecutor from the Ankara National Security Court. Further extension was granted by another judge until the third of December, '97.

Before the end of their police custody period, on November the third, '97 around eleven forty-five PM, the applicants were interrogated. They faced a judge only one day later, the twenty-fourth of the same month, when a judge ordered Çolak’s release during judicial proceedings and kept Sarı in custody.

Following the indictment of 8 December '97 by public prosecutor, the applicants were set as defendants of the National Security Court, charged with being a part of an armed gang, as per Article six-eighty-two of the Criminal Code.

After a trial held 9th June, ‘98, Sarı was given provisional release. In a ruling made in April, second '99, classifying the crime differently, National Security Court found both guilty, aiding & abetting, an offense described under Article sixty-ninety of said code. They were sentenced each to three years nine months in prison along with a ban on holding public office for equal years. 

Later, they both contested the ruling. In a judgment handed February twenty-third '00, the Court of Appeal annulled the verdict due to misclassification of crime. In a further ruling delivered eleventh November '01, the National Security Court postponed its ruling over the case.
0.75.4:
The case started out in 2014 against the Republic of Poland, per an application made by Mr Dariusz Karwowski. The Polish Government took part as represented by their Agent at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ms. J. Chrzanowska in this application. The applicant contended particularly about being subjected to the so-called 'dangerous detainee’ status and its prolonged duration constituting inhumane treatment in violation to the Article 3 of The Convention for Protection of Basic Human Rights and Freedoms. After July the 22nd 2014, the complaint under the Article three of said convention was sent for communication, while rest of it was declared non-admissible by following Rule fifty-four section-three from the Court guidelines.

Mr.Dariusz Karwowski was born around year of 1971, and now he persists under arrest in Warsaw. A. Prior criminal cases Mr Karwowski was apprehended and confined on 2006, being accused of dual murders alongside instigation of another attempted murder against an individual who was intended to testify in another case. Over the years he obtained multiple convictions for different offenses. Particularly, on 2012, he was found guilty and sentenced for murder by the Warsaw High Court. B. Implementation of the 'dangerous detainee' policy On January 24, 2006, the Warsaw Detention and Reform Unit Panel (the panel) determined that he was considered as a 'dangerous detainee'. The stated reason was to place him within a special section or cell designed with enhanced security measures for both public safety and the center’s security. The notice conveyed the detainee’s rights to contest through a seven-day appeal to the Warsaw High Court, X Penitentiary Department. His challenge was not taken forward. The same panel consistently renewed their stance, issuing more than a dozen rulings extending his classification. Each decision adhered broadly similar wording, identifying the necessity to continue the regime due to ongoing risks. On January 3, 2013 ruling extended this status because of the gravity involved with the charges and his poor moral standing. Mr Karwowski's sole objection to the repeated rulings was the 2013 appeal, which was dismissed by the Warsaw High Court on 29 January 2013. The court confirmed the legality of these decisions. On Novemebr,25th , the panel removed his 'dangerous detainee' designation.

In addition to that, his treatment under this regime included constant video surveillance of his cell, requiring him to undress in front of staff each time he went into or out.
0.75.5:
The case started as a complaint from an individual, Mr İlhan Karakurt—a Turkish citizen—against Turkey, submitted in August of the late 90's using the European Commission for Human Rights. At the time, Mr Karakurt had legal counsel named A. Erdoğan. Unfortunately, there were no government representatives for these proceedings. In 2002 January 29, the court partially ruled against accepting the complaint and chose to share concerns surrounding the trial's fairness relating the accused to Turkey's government. Simultaneously, both the admissibility review process and the substantive matter were to happen together, per Article 29§ 3 of the Convention.

In terms of the situation, Mr Karakurt—born the same year as 1960—is currently residing within Turkey. On the 25th May of the year 95, he found himself detained by authorities from a local security office due suspected involvement alongside others in the TDKP/GKB group, a supposed unlawful organization. Following this, he was brought forth at their facility where he was questioned and eventually signed something. He alleged that he was pressured during his signature. 

On the day following, the 28th may 1995, he was presented to a judge who decided on his interim detainment. Subsequently, on June 28 the same year, the prosecutor filed official charges in a Superior Security Court for Izmir under section two of criminal law chapter 168, related to his association with the aforementioned group. Ultimately, on 24 April, 2016, the Superior Security Court in Izmir found him guilty according the accusations and handed him a 12 years 6 month jail term. They also gave a life-time ban from governmental service positions to Mr Karakurt.

On the 4th year of 1996, Mr Karakurt contested but lost in a higher court the same year, and again in the Court of Cassation in the early months of 2000, which signaled the end of appeals. However, despite the ruling, neither Mr Karakurt himself and his attorney were made aware nor notified. On February 23rd, 2005, Mr Karakurt's lawyer informed the court that he had been conditionally released after serving most of a 15-year sentence.
0.75.6: The case began on 3 October 2002 by a Polish citizen by the name of Artur Warsiński challenging the Republic of Poland in regard to human right violations through the European Court of Human Rights (Strasbourg, France). Artur Warsiński was detained starting on March 6, 2002, for charges related to drug trafficking until May, 22nd 2004 in Słupsk Detention Centre. On the fifty-eighth day after his capture, Artur Warsiński was convicted for drug dealing and handed an imprisonment sentence of 1094 days. His appeal was dismissed and the decision made on December the thirtieth of two thousand third by the regional court in Gdańsk. The applicant also claimed that his outgoing mail was being monitored and censored. He mentioned that letters addressed directly and indirectly to the Court of Human Rights were marked "censored," and some even showed signs they have been tampered with. For instance, one envelope sent in October had been cut and sealed back with tape. There is a record indicating that the Słupsk Regional Court at some point wrongly marked the applicant’s correspondence "censored." In response, the applicant wrote to the court, requesting a clarification and received a reply stating that his letters had merely been stamped "censored," and that was a simple administrative error.
0.75.7: The case began following a request in September, 15 2000, by three Polish citizens - Mr Włodzimierz Majewski and Mr Kazimierz Gniłka of Bełchatów and Mr Włodzimierz Strzelczyk hailing from Szczerców - against their country under the Convention for Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms via Article thirty-four of their rights and freedoms. The Polish Government's representatives were Mr. K. Drzewicki early and later by Mr.J. Wołąsiewicz from Foreign Affairs Ministry. The complaint was communicated by the Court on the sixteenth, June in twenty zero three and deemed admissible and its substance would be judged together. On March thirteenth, 1989 the applicants registered an action for payment concerning Bełchatow Coal Mine in the town of Rogowiec through Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki). In November seventeeth of eighteen eighty nine the said court issued ruling, but both sides contested the decision. The Supreme Court overturned the initial ruling and sent it back in March seventh, 1991. In June seventh of nineteen hundred and ninety-three another expert contributed a report to the court. Court sessions took place over these dates: September sixteenth 1993; June twenty-eigth one thousand nine hundred ninety four then again, July twenty-eigth in same year. In that August eleventh, eighteen hundred and ninety-four the Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court passed the judgment. Both the parties lodged an appeal. The Łódź Court of Appeal, in March twenty fourth 1995, overthrew the said judgment and sent this back for reassessment in the lower court. Over these dates, September twenty-six, November fifth and December tenth in nineteen hundred and ninety six alongside June third, nineteen hundred and ninety-seven, the Regional Court conducted further hearings. In the June eleventeenth nineteen hundred 1997 the Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court issued final verdict. The applicants challenged that decision. In December seventeenths, one thousand nine hundred ninety seven the Łódź Court of Appeal revised the original decree and mandated that Bełchatow Coal Mine should compensate applicants a greater sum of money. In February eleventh of two thousand, the applicants filed a higher-level appeal before Supreme Court. The Supreme Court, upon the defendant's legal representative's request, on March sixteenths of same year altered their previous denial of the applicants' higher-level challenge by instructing applicants to cover the costs incurred by the defendant. This ruling became effective for them only after they received formal notice on March twentieth, two thousand of that year.
0.75.8:
The case began due to an application on April 23, 2002 from Mr İlhami Erseven among other individuals challenging Turkey regarding human and fundamental rights under the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, represented through Mr Fevzi Gümüş. No representative was appointed by Turkish government officials. The court partially declared this application inadmissible by June, 14, 2006 but communicated concerns about the fairness in the court hearing process. This declaration came during a dual examination process which included evaluating both admissibility alongside merits.

The background details highlight nine individuals - all born before and between 1958 - who were part of the executive or audit committees for an NGO named Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association. Located predominantly throughout Ankara, İzmir and Istanbul, this group was found non-compliant regarding certain legal requirements during an inspection in November 200, which included failing to maintain proper record keeping as mandated in the Associations Law and not conducting regular reviews as required per the same legislation. These regulatory breaches led to the issuance and imposition of fines in late 2000 and early 2001 by the Ankara public prosecutor. Subsequent to non-payment of fines, a formal indictment was filed against those involved in contravention of the law on associations and criminal code provisions. After conviction by the local magistrates' court in September of said year, appeals were filed by the petitioners arguing for procedural unfairness. These objections were rejected by the first instance criminal court through multiple rulings over the next few months.
0.75.9: The case began on May 6th, 2009 as a human rights application against the Republic of Turkey under the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Semir Güzel from Diyarbakır and a vice-president in HAK-PAR - the Rights and Freedoms Party, contested the actions taken at their congress. In 2004 they held what was said to violate regulations regarding language at a conference, with Mr Güzel recognized as the meeting's chairman. Despite warnings from a superintendent, he allowed Kurdish language to continue in speeches, which led to an indictment against him for breaking a law. The Ankara Criminal Court found him guilty after he did not stop Kurds speaking their native language at his request, sentencing him one year of jail in early February the next year due to these charges. The conviction was later overturned due to procedural issues, and then the court dismissed the case because the legal timeframe to proceed had ended, in 2011.
0.75.10:
The case began when Mr. Hatem İşcan from Turkey filed a complaint against Turkey on 15th Jan 2008 regarding violation under human rights as per the Convention for Human Rights, through Article 34 of the Convention for Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.

The applicant was represented by Mr. A. F. Demirkan based at Bursa and the government was represented by their agent.

On 12 June, the President from the Second Section informed about the application to the government, and also decided on admissibility and merit together simultaneously. 

Mr. Hatem İşcan who lived at Bursa was 69 years of birth in 1937, was involved in land seizure case in 2004, where the Highways department took over the land without any formal process, intending on constructing an express way.

In 2005, the Karacabey Civil Court awarded Mr. Hatem 5500 Turkish lira as compensation, which he then turned to execution procedures to receive his payment.

In the following year, in Nov 2006, the court awarded him 561 million 50 Turkish lira, with interest, for his additional compensation request then went onto execution procedures to collect that sum too (file no:2009/2815).

0.75.11:
The case began from an application lodged against Poland under the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant was a Hungarian man by the surname Woznijk. He had legal representation from a Gdańsk-based lawyer J Danisewicz in his application, sent on June sixth 2006, which alleged the applicant was unlawfully detained for more duration than allowed under human rights law. The Polish government responded to notifications issued to them from the court and proceeded under Article twenty-nine paragraph thirty of the Convention.

The individual in question, Woznijk, who was born in the year '68 was held in custody since the twenty-first of the month July in '01. This arrest was related with a murder charge initially but was amended over subsequent periods. The court's decision to keep him in custody was based mostly because they believed he was likely to avoid legal measures, given potential serious penalties for his actions. Over the period, his detention was repeatedly extended, notably on various dates specifying the judge’s reasoning for each extension. After going through many legal hearings from March 2002 to May of 2002, and again between February and March 2003, he served prison terms in unrelated cases. 

Notably, the appeal Woznijk made against earlier rulings was rejected, and between the years two thousand and five to seven, the case involved fourteen overall hearings in the Gdańsk Regional Court. He remained in custody until May fifteenth two-thousands seven when the regional court finally deemed sufficient evidence had accumulated, concluding his case was nearing its end thereby no longer necessitating his detention beyond that point.
The trial for the original charges continued and remains pending.
0.75.12:
The case began as of May 3rd in the year of twenty thousand when a Polish citizen named Mieczysław Król initiated proceedings through the Article thirty four provision stipulated on the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. He sought legal aid from a lawyer based within the city of Komorów, Poland. Representing the government side was Mr. K. Drzewicki and Mr., J., Wołąsiewicz from Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated via the Court on the 12nd of the month of March 2002.

Mieczysław Król was born and currently resides at Warsaw, Poland. In early stages of February in 1994 he filed a lawsuit against an individual identified only by the name E.K in the Warsaw Regional Court. In early March following said year, a partial waiver of court fees was granted in his favor. A first scheduled hearing took place on the 26th of January in 1995, but it was postponed because of poor health of his adversary.

They proceeded to multiple hearings on the dates of third March, eighteen April, sixth June and finally the third of October and sixteenth January along with sixteenth of April later on. Witnesses and E.K. herself testified throughout. On April the sixteenth in 1996, an expert witness was appointed and their evaluation was received shortly after on May tenth, nineteen ninety-six. The court conducted additional hearings on September nineteenth of 1996, with the inclusion of expert testimonies.

In April 2000, the applicant petitioned for a fresh expert opinion and asked to expedite proceedings due to his own health issues. An expert was indeed appointed on October twenty-eighth that year to provide an independent opinion. By July seventeenth in one thousand nine hundred ninety-eight he requested a rescheduling of the hearings due to the infrequency of sessions. This continued into various stages of 2000, including court hearings in March and November. The court ultimately obtained opinions from experts and ruled on the matter in the winter and spring seasons respectively, leading to judgments by the Regional court on November 7 and Court of Appeal on January the 20th of twenty-first century, with further appeals pending before the highest judicial authority.
0.75.13:
The case began from 12 September, 2007 by a Danish citizen named Mr Rolf Nielsen, who applied through the Article 34 of the Convention of Human Rights to the Kingdom of Denmark. Mr Nielsen was assisted during these proceedings via a lawyer based from Copenhagen and the government side was represented by Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen from Ministry of Justice.

This new concept "tax asset stripping", introduced the early to mid-nineties, was characterized by criminal activities involving buying inactive solvent private companies and stripping off their assets for personal gain. Around one thousand six hundred companies were stripped between the 80s' late period till mid-90, accumulating a total tax debt exceeding 2 billion Danish kroner, which turned into a significant number of lawsuits related liability of the banks, buyers and professional advisors like accountants and lawyers.

In the fall 1992, Mr Nielsen sold his company called Soft TUX Aps, which was rechristened to HOP no 49. Then in the spring of 1995 HOP no 49 declared bankruptcy. A trustee was assigned the responsibility of winding things up. In October 1997, the trustee initiated a suit against Mr Nielsen and a bank named BG Bank A/S demanding over four and a half million Danish kroner in compensation.

Following this, in 1998, BG Bank A/S joined the suit and filed claims against Mr Nielsen alongside other professionals such as an accounting firm and two lawyers. In response to the misleading advice provided by the bank and the legal team, Mr Nielsen started a separate case against those professionals. Over a period, the case saw numerous hearings, exchanges of pleadings, adjournments, and the involvement of multiple legal representatives until 2008.

The central issue of the case concerned the potential liability of the buyer, the buyer bank, their lawyers and accountants over the misadvised actions during the sale of companies which led to their bankruptcy. Despite several adjustments and extensions, the main trial took place starting the fall in the year of 2008, followed by a final judgment passed in December of the following year.
0.75.14:
The case started in July of 2007 in an application against the Republic of Poland submitted in accordance to Articles 34 of the Convention for Protecting Human Rights by a Polish resident named Adam Matoń. Matoń's representative, Mr.J. Wołąsiewicz, who worked for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, stood against the government during the proceedings at the Fourth Section. On 28 June 2008 the court notified both parties. The application would now be considered for admissibility, as well as its merits. The details of his case will be found later. In brief, the case concerns an individual named Mr Matoń (born after 1950; lived at that point in Kraków; no specific year or precise name provided) facing criminal charges including drug trafficking and unlawful possession of firearms. Matoń was part of alleged organized crime. Matoń appeared in court for the first time in February of a subsequent year (year not specified). Over roughly four years starting after his initial court appearance, the court conducted about twice as much hearings as in his first visit. On the 2008-02-13 date Matoń's case was judged in his absence and he was found guilty. Subsequently, Matoń appealed and the case is ongoing through the Katowice Regional Court.

For a separate but related matter, Matoń filed a complaint regarding his timely trial under a 2004 Act stipulating conditions for such complaints. In 2005 Matoń challenged court proceedings, claiming compensation (amount unspecified); however the Katowice Court of Appeal rejected it due to length of proceedings, stating that although lengthy, this did not fall under the described conditions and delays were due mostly to outside circumstances. A second appeal in Matoń's case was dismissed as well, with the ruling indicating numerous postponements because of various factors like unavailability or illness among the involved parties and staff. Furthermore, it mentioned that the case was of considerable complexity, and court efforts towards quick resolution were noted.
0.75.15:
The document details the case of Selim Ünay who, born 1958, resided in Kandıra at the time. Ünay's arrest occurred on 9th of July, 1996 as part of a bank robbery operation. Transferred to the Istanbul State Security Court, he was detained and indicted the 24th July for alleged unlawful armed group membership disrupting state governance. The case progressed through several trials, showing repeated accusations and refusals of bail due to ongoing investigation. His conviction initially carried a life sentence but was overturned. He faced retrial, again resulting in his conviction under the same charges and sentence. However, this decision too was reversed, leading the case to continue. With the abolishment of the State Security Courts in a constitutional change effective in May 7,2004, the case transitionally moved to the Istanbul Assize Court but remained unresolved and he continued imprisonment awaiting further proceedings.
The final status mentioned states that the case was ongoing; the applicant, Selim Ünay as of the write-up, is still held under custody.
0.75.16:
The application came into the Court's purview pursuant to an application lodged through a process outlined Article 34 of the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, by Jan Kachel of Polish nationality. The application was filed against Republic Poland and was received by the Court on 17th of May. The Polish Government was represented during proceedings. The applicant claimed his pre-trial detention exceeded permissible limits under Article 5 section three. On the 17th day of May in the year 2005, Mr Jan Kachel was detained on charges of murder. Initially, on July 30, 2002 he got arrested, and on July 31st the same year, Bytom District Court decided to holdhim in custody. The reasons mentioned were the severity and seriousness related with the crime, the strong evidence pointing fingers in Kachel, the potential for harsh punishment and ensuring smooth justice. His appeal was denied. 

In mid-September 4 of the same year, the Katowice Regional Court agreed with the District Court's decision, reiterating that detention was due. Further extension of his detention was then granted on multiple occasions - October2nd, December2nd, March 31st, July2nd and June16th. Post reaching two-year limit set in Code of Criminal Procedure, the initial authority could not prolong detention anymore and so, Katowice Court of Appeal took up the matter on July 14 of2004, December8,2004, April 6th of same year and December28,0f 05. Detention was again prolonged. Justifications for these included the gravity, strong evidence, risk of tampering with justice, need of extensive hearing from numerous witnesses along with expert opinion. Towards the end of the period, complexity of the case was cited along with the prevalence of strong evidence. Meanwhile, on April 16 in of the year 2003, the applicant was indicted with murder and his accomplices. Finally, on July4in of2005, the Katowice Regional Court pronounced its verdict convicting him alongwith his accomplices, sentencing him to a term of imprisonment for a duration of25years. 0.75.17:
The case began in a complaint made against Poland through an application (no date specified but lodged in late 2006), submitted according to Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection and Promotion Human Rights. The applicant, Mr. Paweł Gradek (born and residing details provided), claimed his rights, specifically regarding family life, had suffered infringement. 0.75.18: The case started following application 3042/05 by a Turkish citizen, Nihat Konak, submitted under Article 34 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (the Convention)'s guidelines in November, 2004. Mr M.A. Kırdök represented Konak. Konak is currently incarcerated in the Tekirdağ Prison. On 1998, March 26 after certain items were seized and a house search, Konak got into police custody due suspected involvement with TKP/ML-TIKKO (Communists of Turkey / Marxist-Leninist Turkish Workers and Peasants' Liberation Army), an illegal organization. Konak claimed he was interrogated without legal representation and refused to respond. During the interrogation he was not given counsel. On that same March day, co-accused L.L.'s description matched Konak as both the Marmara District Secretary and head of Istanbul's organization. On March, April 2nd, a medical report was filed; noting no physical harm besides three individuals including L.L.. L.L experienced a minor injury on her back and face. The same day Konak appeared for questioning at the Istanbul State Security Court without legal representation. He denied the accusations and refused the confrontation and identification reports. As a result he stayed incarcerated. On April, 22nd the Istanbul Public Prosecutor indicted him on charges related to leading an armed group. Released on July sixth 1998, on October fifteenth the year 2001 he was found guilty and imprisoned on November nineteenth the same year. On February fourteenth the following year, the Court of Cassation overturned that verdict for insufficient elaboration, but on December 26 the Istanbul State Security Court reaffirmed the conviction, sentencing Konak eighteen years. They noted that certain co-defendants identified him as the district leader, and found he participated actively through illegal acts. On May twenty-fifth the Court of Cassation confirmed that conviction.
0.75.19: The case began from a complaint filed under the Convention for Protection against the Republic Turkey on June 1, 1991 by Anna Evagorou Christou of Cyprus who received legal aid from A. Demetriades based from Nicosia. The government's representative is Z.M. Necatigil. The applicant claimed the Turkish invasion took possession her home and property. On August 24 of the previous year the court decided this was an admissible complaint. Both parties provided their observations and third-party input was received from the government of Cyprus. The applicant, born 1925 and residing now at Nicosia, resided once along with immediate family members within Kalogrea in Kyrenia District. During the 1974 incident, Turkish military expelled the applicant plus her kin, compelling them to head for the southern region. Up until September the 9,1999, when the properties were transferred over for her children, she owned ten plots of land in Kalogrea, inclusive two houses. One of that abode belonged with the applicant and was constructed back in the 1916. Comprising spacey rooms, two bedrooms, a living area, a kitchen and a bathroom, it had two levels, a large courtyard, was composed using stone, adorned with marble floors, titled roof and wooden doors and windows. Another house was the applicant’s leisure retreat from '58 and lay near the seaside. As supporting documents, the applicant supplied statements of ownership from the Department of Lands and Surveys of the Republic of Cyprus, confirming that she was the legal and registered proprietor of such two dwellings alongside lots numbered 260 to 425. Certificates of the registration of eight out of total ten sites were also provided for. The applicant contended she could never recapture her home and properties since the Turkish military utilized and barricaded these. On December 9 the same year the applicant attempted returning to her home and property in Kyrenia and village Kalogrea through a convoy of fellow displaced persons. The organizers of this convoy advised the UN forces stationed in Cyprus of such intentions previously. The convoy halted at a checkpoint in 'buffer zone', the main route connecting Nicosia to Famagusta. They approached a UN officer, requesting permission, and instructed them too to communicate with the Turkish military about their situation. The officer declined their request, citing refusal by the military.
0.75.20: The case began with an application from a Turkish citizen against Turkey on July 8th 2002, according to the provisions set in the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental freedoms. The individual, named Yusuf Salduz, was represented legally, though the government did not send representatives despite being asked. The application detailed Salduz's arrest on 29 May, 2001. He was detained and questioned by authorities who accused him of involvement during an unauthorized protest supporting the PKK, an organization that has been outlawed in the country and a party to armed conflict. Salduz initially confessed under police questioning; but later, while in court, he recanted that confession. On the following day of his initial arrest, the court ordered his continued detention pending investigation. On June first of same year, Salduz faced the prosecutor and judge, claiming his confession was coerced, a claim they disregarded as they proceeded to decide on his case. By July, formal charges were filed against him, leading eventually in December, when the State Security Court convicted Salduz of assisting and aiding the PKK and sentenced his sentence. Given his young age at time, the sentence was reduced. The conviction was based largely on a report about the handwriting match between Salduz's and the placard's writing, as well as testimony from Salduz's co-defendants that he had organized their participation during the demonstration. There was also mention of the report stating Salduz was among the crowd dispersing afterwards. Later, the Prosecutors' office submitted a report to the Court of Cassation, endorsing the previously mentioned verdict, and this decision was upheld on the 9th June in a subsequent hearing.
0.75.21:
The case came up because someone called Mr. Władysław Godysz filed an appeal in Poland on September 3, 2007 under the rules that protect basic rights according to an international pact called "Convention." His lawyer's office was based where people treated coal in Katowice, while a man working with foreign affairs in Poland handled their side during discussions with the court. Mr Władysław Godysz was kept in jail while they looked through his actions because he possibly took bribes among other major wrongdoings. The court thought it needed help from him for the case, saying more people were involved than usual making it complicated; they were worried he'd try to hide facts from the truth or change stories.

The investigation led arrests for over two dozen people including our main person; all their requests for freedom failed. He was set to pay money to go back and forth until April 10th, when the amount went down significantly from 800k Polish zlotys to 30k. Finally, after paying the lower sum, he got to leave on April 3rd 2008.

0.75.22:
The case began on April 29, 2003 when a Turkish national, Cahit Demirel, filed an application against Turkey based on the Convention for Protection of Human Rights. He sought legal relief on issues surrounding his arrest, detention, and trial process. His legal representatives were M. Beştaş, practicing lawyers.

For his alleged involvement, Cahit, who resides in Batman since birth, was apprehended on April 1st and suspected of PKK (Workers' Party of Kurdistan) activities. He faced charges of being a member under Article 168 of the previous Criminal Code in a public prosecutor's report, which was submitted to the Diyarbakır State Security Court on an unspecified date, after the Batman public prosecutor made no jurisdiction determination and forwarded the casefile on May the following year.
  
At Diyarbakır's State Security Court on the 25th day of December the year 2001, he received his conviction. Despite numerous requests, the court consistently declined to release Cahit during his preliminary hearings, considering the seriousness of his alleged crime. The judgement was overturned by the Court of Cassation in early autumn 2002, resulting the case being returned.

Cahit was freed on May the year thereafter upon a release order from Diyarbakır State Security Court. However, the court reconvened and re-convicted him on March of year two-thousand-four, reaffirming his punishment under Article of the old Criminal Code. This decision too was reversed by a higher court.

With Law 5190, effective June 2nd of this year, State Security Courts were abolished, and the trial against Cahit was reassigned to the Diyarbakır Assize Court, where the tribunal concluded that the legal process had expired due to time limitations by June 2005.
0.75.23:
The case stemmed initially via application (number 20491/92), filed in 1992 against Switzerland, by Mr. Rajko Medenica, a Yugoslavian-American, with the European Commission of Human Rights, based upon violations of Article 6 §§1 of the Convention of Human Rights. Medenica, deceased as early as 1997, was represented by legal counsel, including Mr. C. Poncet; his widow and children continued the case as his legal successors. The Swiss Government was represented by Mr P. Boillat, part of the International Affairs Division from Federal Office of Justice.

Medenica claimed his trial in absentia violated his right to a fair trial as delineated per Article 6 §§1 of Convention. The application was submitted to the Court on 1998 when Protocol Number Eleven to the Convention became operational.

The Court's reception of the application was not immediately definitive and the case was assigned to the Second Section of the Court. The Chamber assessing the matter was formatted according to established procedures.

Medenica arrived Switzerland in late sixties and obtained medical credentials in 1970. He worked as a physician in a Geneva hospital, focusing on international relations and care of Yugoslav patients from 73. 

On 71, Medenica faced charges for financial deceit involving the welfare system of his home country, Serbia. Law enforcement initiated investigations, followed by Medenica's detention in 82 and bail release in early 84. Medenica emigrated for US, gaining citizenship and resumed practice.

In 85, Medenica was to face trial in Geneva for fraud but avoided it, only returning to the court's jurisdiction in 89. A series of hearings were scheduled, but Medenica could not appear before the trial due to a restraining order from the US District Court. This order forbade his departure and required his return to the US for examination by the court.

Despite requests for a postponement, Medenica refused to appear in absentia, and the Geneva Assize Court proceeded with his trial in his absence on 26 April ’89, convicting him and sentencing him to four years in prison.
0.75.24: Mr Hıdır Ateş, the editor-in-chief at Yedinci Gündem - and Ms Hünkar Demirel, whose newspaper it owned, both from Istanbul, faced charges following publishing an article in their newspaper featuring an interview with Cemil Bayık - a PKK leader. The interview criticized the government actions and called for the European Court of Human Rights' intervention for Kurdish rights. Following this, they were charged for allowing the publication of an illegal armed organization's statements in August of 2001 by the Istanbul State Security Court. They were sentenced to heavy fines in early December; the sentence included a brief closure period of the newspaper. Their appeal was dismissed, and by summer of that same year, the closure of the newspaper was enforced by local authorities.
0.75.25: The case began from a 2001 application lodged in the Court through Article 34 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms against the Republic of Turkey, by Mr Oguz Atakan Koseoglu of Turkey, who was represented legally and lived in Izmir at birth (1951). 0.75.26: Four Turkish individuals—Ms. Meyrem Gültekin (1952 birthyear) and Mr. Naci Güncü (born 1960, Mr. Taci Güncü from a later year in his 30s), and Ms Feriha Demircan who was born earlier than all three men—lodged proceedings under Articles 34 of Europe’s Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms following the taking-over of their property by Turkish authorities. 0.75.27:
The case involved Turkish citizens who worked in Diyarbakır for Diyarbakır Sur Municipality but had their employment terminated on a certain day in May 1999, resulting in unpaid wages. 0.75.28:
The case began after Mr. Antoni Sibilski applied on behalf of himself (a Polish citizen), against the Republic of Poland, to seek relief based under the Convention for protection against human rights and fundamental freedoms violations on or before Mar 9 2000 according to the Article 34 provision. The Polish Government was represented during this court process. Communication of this application occurred on Jun 16 2003, and the Court then proceeded to consider both its admissibility criteria and the underlying facts of merit.

The key details surrounding this legal dispute show that Mr Antoni Sibilski was born in the year 1957 living within the place called Jarocin. He formally filed paperwork requesting a divorce on Apr 20th1993 to the Poznań Regional Court. That court convened several meetings including ones on Aug. 23th 1993, Oct 7 1993, Jan.30th, and April 10 1994. A professional evaluation was later ordered by them on Jun 2 1994 which was received on Aug 29 th 1994. More sessions followed on Nov.8 20th, Feb 28th, 4th April , Aug .9 th and Nov.3 25 th1 995. A revised request for his legal claim came on Jun .3 5th 1996; and he accepted the other party retaining custodial rights on Sep.8 19th. Further examination of the legal dispute was requested on Sep.5th 1996, by the court, directing the Psychological Department of Poznań University to provide findings on his child’s emotional growth. Delaying the process, the hearing was adjourned on Jan.7th, 27th and a resubmission of files and opinions was sought from the department on Jan 8 24th 17th. But the department did not comply and sent no report. Concerns over the prolonged proceedings, Mr. Antoni Sibilski expressed dissatisfaction to the Ministry of Justice on Apr 11th 5th and in response, on Jun.15th, 17th the ministry assessed the situation and acknowledged his complaints.

Proceedings continued with hearings held between Jun.18th 25th and Nov.6 th,1 1998. Another complaint of delay was made by him in June 21st 23rd 1998. 0.75.29:
The case started through Mr. Ryszard Panusz filing an application in early October 2001, against the Polish government, using Article 34 from the European Convention on Human Rights. The case began in a complaint filed on behalf of Mrs Ayten Ünal Tekeli with the European Commission of Human Rights against the Republic of Turkey regarding a violation of her rights as a Turkish national. Mrs Ayten Ünal Tekeli received legal aid through this process.

Mrs Ayden Demirel Ersezen, from İzmir, represented Mrs Ünal Tekeli while the Turkish Government (hereafter referred to as The Government), were represented through their legal agent in the case. 

Mrs Ünal Tekeli contended in this case that the domestic courts' refusal allowed her to adopt a mere maiden surname was an unjustifiable infringement upon her right to private and family life as guaranteed within article eight(8).

She argued that married men had an exception by being able retain only their birth surnames. This alleged discrimination was based around her interpretation of article fifteen(15) of the Turkish Civil Code and article fourteen(4) of the Convention respectively and its implications.

Mrs Ünal Tekeli's application came in on December the twenty-first of one thousand nine hundred and ninety-five. It was received by the European Court of Human Rights on the first day of November nineteen hundred and ninety-eight when protocol number eleven to the Convention entered into force.

At the time, the application was allocated by the court's fourth section according the rule fifty-two section one. When the court's composition was revised on the first day of November two thousand and one (Rule 25 section), the newly reconstituted fourth section took this case.

In a decision rendered by a chamber on July one, two thousand and three the application was declared admissible.

The case was heard at the Human Rights Building in Strasbourg on January thirteen, four thousand and four. The proceedings were presided by Mrs Deniz Akcay, Mrs Burçe Arı, Mrs Işık Batmaz Keremoğlu and Mrs Banur Özaydın.

Mrs Aydan Demirel Ersezen and Mr Hayati Torun represented the applicant during proceedings and she was present herself at hearing.

Mrs Ünal Tekeli, described as a trainee lawyer, married on the twenty-fifth day of the month of December in nineteen hundred and ninety. She maintained the surname Ünal, her maiden surname in her professional life.

Following her marriage, Mrs Ünal Tekeli was legally required (pursuant Article 15 of the Turkish Civil Code) to carry the surname of her spouse, Ünal Tekeli.

Though she used both maiden surnames professionally, she was unable to use them together officially.

On the twenty-second February in nineteen hundred and ninety-five the applicant sought a court order (at the Karşıyaka Court of First Instance) allowing the use only the maiden name Ünal.

The court rejected this request on the grounds stipulated (under Article 153) by the Turkish Civil Code, which states that married women should bear the surname of a husband for entirety life.

An appeal was filed and rejected again by the Court of Cassation on six June in nineteen hundred and ninety-five.

A modification to the provisions related by Article one hundred fifty-three of the Turkish Civil Code on the fourteenth May nineteen hundred and ninety-seven allowed married women to use their maiden names at the beginning of husband's surnames. Despite this change, Mrs Ünal Tekeli declined the option as she found it insufficient.

The main facts include Ms. Seweryn living in Warsaw who faced issues regarding payments against the Adwokat Housing Co-operative in '99. Initially, the district court did not process her request to join her case and finally, in Oct of '22, they deemed her case separate and returned her claim due to errors, leading to appeals. By '08, the final judgment was by chance as the court disregarded procedural errors. Several appeals and further hearings continued into '09, with cases being postponed multiple times until a default judgment was issued on '08's May, followed closely after by making this judgment effective immediately.

In '08, Seweryn also filed an objection against this default judgment and another hearing was held in '29. Further hearings in '08 and '09 also took place but the matter is still pending. Seweryn also complained in '08 to the Warsaw Regional Court about the unreasonable delay in proceedings under a '2004 law' wherein she asked for PLN 100 thousand or equivalent EUR as damages. However, the court declined her complaint in '08, primarily focusing more upon her own actions rather than the court's handling.
0.75.70:
The case began due to four Turkish citizens—Mr Dede, Mr Kumral, Mr Hakkı, Zabcı, Mr Akın and Mr Dirik—who filed claims to the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article of 25 of the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms between mid-May 1996, and the first week in June the next year regarding unfair treatment. Mr Dede had legal representation from Ms Nurten Çaglar and Mr Mehdi Bektaş, however, Mr Kumral's and Mr Zabcı's cases were pursued independently.

The defendants were accused under Article six section one of the Convention for lengthy trials. The application reached the Court on the first of November in 1998 with the implementation of Protocol number eleventh to the said Convention and was managed initially as part of Section One. 

The applicants and officials made formal statements before the Court. The facts indicated that in January to February of '81 the applicants were detained by the police and charged as members of an illegal organization named Dev-Yol. Subsequently, they were remanded to custody three times in April and July of the same year, according to decisions rendered by the Ankara Martial Law Court. 

All were, subsequently, released on bail pending their trial. Post the lifting of Martial Law, their cases were heard at the Ankara Martial Law Court where they were found guilty on the 19th day of July '89. They appealed to the Military Court of Cassation. 

Following the abolition of the martial courts through legislation passed Dec '94, the appellate process shifted entirely into the hands of ordinary courts. The Court of Cassation upheld the verdict of Mr Kumral but dismissed those of Mr Dede, and Mr Dirik, directing their cases to the Ankara Heavy Criminal Court. An update on this matter suggests the proceedings are ongoing in this court.
The case has been moved to a new Section due the reorganization on Nov '01.
0.75.71: The case began on 2001-12-19 where Mr. Bogdan Dzierzanowski from Poland filed application (no number) against Republic Poland concerning the Convention for Human Rights. The Polish government was represented during the process by Mr. J. Wołasiwicz on 2005-08-24. On this date, the application was communicated, and the case's admissible and substantive examination were considered simultaneously due to Article 29 §3. Details about the applicant include birth in Poland on 1966 and residence in Białystok since then until the incident. On the 22nd Dec 1992, a car accident occurred causing one fatality in which he participated. Following the accident, an investigation was initiated, but it got discontinued in Mar 1993. Then an auxiliary prosecutor requested a restart, leading the investigation to continue. By Mar 11,1994, the applicant faced charges for manslaughter despite not being informed as he left before. He stood before the Białystok District Court on 030 Jun and was further heard on several dates from Sep to Dec in '96 and '97. In 1998, there continued hearings in Feb, Apr, Sep and Oct. On October, 2008, the Białystok District Court released its verdict, where he was declared not guilty. The case then went for appeal on Feb, '99, and the appellate court reversed the first verdict and remanded it back. The district court reconvened a meeting Nov 16 in 1999. In 2000, a single hearing took place Jan 28, followed by a directive to procure an expert opinion. On May 14, another session was conducted. Finally, on the day of June, 8, the applicant admitted his guilt, and he received a suspended prison term. The final sentencing was in line with this verdict.
0.75.72:
The case arose from the application of a Polish national named Mr Dariusz Karykowski on the 27 of December in the Year 2011, against The Republic Of Poland. The application was made through Article Thirty-Four of what is called the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant received legal aid and was represented through a lawyer Mr T. Bąk. The Polish Government was represented at this stage of the proceedings through their Agent, Ms J. Chrzanowska, of their Ministry Of Foreign Affairs. The applicant claimed a violation according the third rule of The Convention, which relates to the living conditions of prisoners.

Investigations showed he is a revisited member of the justice system. He was apprehended on an unspecified event due to accusations of making threats. Subsequently, he was found guilty, leading to three years, six months in prison sentence. Initially, he stayed at Nowogard Prison but was later moved over to Goleniów Prison. 

On September eighth, 2011, the prison officials applied a special containment protocol, also known as a "dangerous detainee" regimen towards this individual. This was based, in part on the thought that he orchestrated a potential mass disagreement within the prison due to an anti-code letter written and signed by 135 fellow inmates. This document criticized new rules concerning the possibility to shop when visiting the prison. In response, the applicant denied orchestrating the protest, saying he simply signed among a number of others. 

A court ruling on November twenty-ninth, the same year, upheld his initial detention under this protocol. Yet, on the twelfth month, the regime was extended because it was deemed the inmate posed an ongoing threat and needed to remain in isolation. An appeal was filed on behalf of this prisoner, and the Superior Court overturned parts but not fully, stating past circumstances did not support such continued restrictions. By February fourteenths of 2012, the protocol no longer applied as the temporary measures were lifted.

In summary, Mr.Dariusz Karykowski was subjected solely for five months plus an additional week and a day to this special containment policy.
0.75.73:
The case began when Turkish citizens Mr Adem Dost (born 1956 and living in Germany, Munich), Mr Şeker Dost born 1954, and Mr Osman Cinel who were also born 1955, filed a complaint via Article 34 of the Convention for Protection on Nov 16th 1998 against Turkey. They were represented legal counsel Ibrahim Gemici practicing law out of Istanbul. The Turkish government did not appoint their legal representative. On 17 June 2004 the Court communicated the complaint to them. In June the same year, the Court informed them they'd be handling admission along with the merits of it. 

In 1995, the Sakarya Governor's office took possession of the land owned individually by Mr Adem and Şeker Dost and Mr Osman Cinel. An evaluation was done by a panel of experts who appraised and compensated these men. When they sought more compensation, the Sakarya Civil Court awarded an extra 86,526,7950 Turkish liras including interest at a rate confirmed from early December, 1995. During hearings, the court visited site and received three opinions on the land type. These consultants deemed the land development. Yet the Court of Cassation's ruling considered nearby land as agricultural thus disregarding their evaluations and opting rather on one expert report for final tally. The applicants challenged this decision in higher courts. The Court of Cassation confirmed the initial judgment in February '98. By mid-April 1998, the Sakarya Governor's office paid them 1,253,621,099 Turkish liras. Their appeal for a correction by the Court of Cassation was denied by end-May 98.
In summary, the issue centered round the evaluation and compensation process following land expropriation by Turkish authorities, the subsequent legal battles, and the final resolution by the Court of Cassation.

The Court communicated to the government on the 28thJanuary of three thousand and three about the duration concerns in legal proceedings. Before the 5th of May in two thousand and three:

- On March nineth, first hearing took place; on April sixth they filed counterclaims.

- Both the hearing scheduled April twentieth and May eighteenth of nineteen ninety-four were cancelled due to health reasons.
- They requested specific dates for settlement talks from January eighteenth, nineteen ninety-five onwards.  
- Hearings between June twenty-first to March seventeen, nineteen ninety-seven, then again in January nineteenth of nineteen ninety-eight and so forth till April twentieth of nineteen ninety-eight were held after a gap.
- In 1999, any change in the panel of judges occurred.

0.75.76:
The case began due an application made through Article 34 of the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by a Polish citizen Katarzyna Gnatowska. She was assisted by lawyer M. Gąsiorowska from Warszawa in her legal proceedings. The Polish Government was represented in court proceedings during this case. The application was notified in mid-2007 to the Government. The court decided to address issues on both admissibility of and reasons for the application simultaneously as per Article 29, paragraph three of the Convention rules.

In the background of facts, Katarzyna's mother initiated a lawsuit against the partition of co-ownership and inheritance in 1986 in Nowy Dwór Mazowiecki District Court involving Katarzyna. Over nearly eight years of legal battles, including fifteen sessions and the appointment by the court of multiple expert witnesses, the initial trial was halted. The case was revitalized later. Further hearings, postponed for different reasons such as gathering more evidence, and three adjournments based at the applicant’s request continued from summer of year one thousand nine hundred and ninety-five till late May in twenty second century. The final session in May of two thousand two did not issue an immediate judgement but ordered further investigation. In July next year, the same court relaunched discussions and requested more evidence, like expert assessments. Then, in November twenty-second, Katarzyna's sibling passed and the process was paused until at least the next year. Operations resumed and four experts were consulted over period extending to June in the two-thousands. The legal proceedings remain unresolved today as of that date.

Katarzyna also utilized another legal avenue when she brought forward a complaint under the June 2004 Act concerning unreasonable delays in judicial proceedings to the Warsawa regional tribunal on 2005 September the 5th. She asked for recognition of prolonged case duration and a sum equivalent to approximately two thousand five hundred euros. However, the regional court declined the claim saying there seemed no blatant breaches of the right-to-a-trial-limitation prior to the new law's implementation date. The court recognized general case slowness, but did not review events leading before September the seventeenth, 2004. Notably, the 2004 Act applied exclusively if cases were still in process after the act's introduction date.

The application came forth via a petition from a Turkish individual, Mr. Cüneyt Mehmet Barker ("the applicant"), against the Republic of Turkey through Articles of the Convention for Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention"). The case was initiated in 2003 and represented legally by a lawyer in Istanbul named K. Koç; the government responded through an agent. In October 2007 the Court announced notice to the government. At that stage the Court aimed for simultaneous ruling about both admissibility of application along with the merits (Article 29 § 3).

The applicant, born on 1949 and residing in Istanbul, claimed ownership rights for some land on Aug 15 in 1988 by filing lawsuit versus Treasury. Despite numerous inquiries, the applicant did find conclusive resolution until 98, when the Court of Cassation revealed a prior judgment on Oct. 28 1992. The case file went missing, as per Erdek Civil Court's statement following the applicant's request. The Treasury asked for rectification on May. 8 of year '98, but the Court of Cassation refused due insufficient reconstituted file and instructed sending the original back.

0.75.78:
The case began when Sławomir Małasiewicz filed his application with the European Court of Human Rights (Article 34, Convention for the Protection of Human Rights) against his native nation, the Republic of Poland, in mid-May of two thousand two, alleging violations of his rights following a workplace accident. Mr Sławomir Małasiewicz resided then (and still does) within the borders of Częstochowa. In June of nineteen hundred and ninety five he was injured at the start of one of his working days, after accidentally rupturing an unopened bottle of sparkling mineral water; the metal cap from said bottle struck his left eye, causing irreversible damage even after he received medical care and corrective surgeries. Consequently, he was recognized as disabled, receiving a pension from the Social Security Board (Zakład Ubezpieczeń Społecznych), Poland's national insurance agency. Seeking recompense, in August nineteen hundred ninety-seven Małasiewicz initiated civil litigation demanding monetary compensation as well as a pension from the producer of the faulty beverage, submitting official health records from hospitals in Częstochowa and Katowice. The Częstochowa Regional Court soon waived his obligation for litigation costs.

A legal process followed, involving various stages and multiple hearings over several years. Witnesses were heard, medical assessments were conducted, and different opinions were presented in chambers. Protracted gaps punctuated this period between formal court meetings, yet there was persistent activity and occasional delays. By the end, in late two thousand two, the Częstochowa Regional Court made its ruling in favor of the plaintiff, ordering the defendant to pay compensation and dismissing his pension claim entirely as unsubstantiated or irrelevant, and sending the case to higher review. Thereby, an appeal was lodged, driven by both parties, yet the appeal proceedings continued unresolved.
0.75.79: The case began in late summer when a Polish citizen named Stefan Kozłowski filed an application on July 10, 2004 with the European Court of Human Rights, contesting actions against him by Poland under human rights protections. The Polish authorities were represented in court by Mr. J. Wołąsiewicz from their Ministry of Foreign Affairs, who faced challenges in responding effectively. A second criminal case was initiated around the same time, but specific details such as the charges, court rulings, dates of hearings or the exact conviction are not provided beyond mentions by Kozłowski's side that he was found guilty. The case started as an application in the European Court of Human Rights on behalf of an unnamed Polish citizen, Mr Jończyk, who claimed unlawful detention awaiting psychiatric transfer to a hospital. The case was initiated via the Convention for Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on 10th Apr 08.

The Polish Government represented the state through Mr J. Wołąsiewicz. Specifically, the applicant argued they were unjustifiably confined in conventional detention till moving to a psychiatric institution. On September 09th, 08, the application was officially notified; admission to both the Court’s admissibility process and its meritorious review was granted the same day.

In terms of the factual background, Jończyk, born post-1976 and currently under custody, was initially apprehended on December, 7th for making threats and domestic abuse allegations. Subsequent to being locked on 8th Dec 07 due to an investigation order issued by the Żary District Court, Jończyk was admitted to a psychiatric unit on the 22nd of Dec, diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia. Released on January,2st, 2008, the court revisited the case on the aforementioned date, finding Jończyk guilty as charged but deemed unfit due to his mental condition. Consequently, he would serve his sentence in a psychiatric facility. The court denied his bail request, citing potential reoffending risk. The detention period was extended by the Żary District Court until 09th Sep. 08, adding that he was at risk of committing further crimes, necessitating continuous detention until psychiatric admission. Jończyk experienced multiple placements over different facilities including Nowa Sól Detention Centre and Zielona Góra Regional Court.

On May 02nd, 2008, the Supreme Court instructed the lower court examining if a pending appeal was filed correctly. Zielona Góra Regional Court adjudicated on 02nd Jul. 2008, affirming the original detention order. The Żary District Court directed Jończyk towards Lubiąż Psychiatric Hospital on July 7, 2008, with admittance scheduled on the 15th of Sept 08, although his discharge was undocumented, occurring sometime before February,09.

In late '90s, the construction company initiated two civil actions—first in 1990 against Devlet Su İşleri over unpaid contract costs, then another in 1995 to recoup further arrears. 0.75.82:
The case stemmed from a complaint (no. 72754/11), filed as per Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights by Uktam Musaev—a citizen of Uzbekistan—who had been living illegally in the Republic of Turkey starting from the year 2008 until 2 April 2011. Musaev was apprehended by law enforcement while investigating an unnamed individual or group suspected involvement in a murder, and was detained under the Yedikule Security Directorate. After delivering a witness statement before the relevant criminal court on 4 April of this year, he remained detained due to overstaying the period allowed within Turkey. On 5 of March, he relocated to the Fatih police station and stayed in a holding cell there. On April tenth, he faced deportation to the Kumkapı Removal Centre. This facility reportedly suffered from extreme overcrowding, and Musaev shared quarters with a large number—between 24 to an astounding count of 45 others—in cramped conditions, almost 30-35 square meters. Hygiene was poor amid such density. There was a significant insect infestation, and the food rations were substandard both by quality and quantity, coupled with lack of recreational space.

On 12 April 11th, Musaev applied to the UNHCR for refugee status, and a few days later on 27 of same month, he sought asylum through the Ministry of Internal Affairs. On 29 the same month, he was granted a temporary residency in the Aksaray province as a pending asylum seeker and was consequently freed from Kumkapı removal center. Subsequent records show that he moved on to reside in Konya. The current information indicates that his plea for asylum along with his application for refugee status continue to await decisions and resolutions at national and international levels alike.
Note: Adjusting the date from "April of same year" to "same month" for clarity and accuracy in narrative flow.
0.75.83:
The case stemmed from a complaint (case no not provided due to redaction) by a citizen from Montenegro against the Swiss government, filed through the Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms Convention. The complainant, Mr Srdan Pesukic, was represented legally when contesting his conviction based partially due to testimony from unidentified witnesses. This complaint was acknowledged on Nov.26.2009, and reviewed alongside its admissibility. Mr. Pesukic was found guilty, serving a jail sentence in Switzerland.

In late October 2001 just past midnight, N.B experienced a fatal shooting near Zurich-Schwamendingen. Suspected of the act was Mr. Pesukic. Two witness interviews took place via a sound system in 2002, where the witness' voice was obscured, preserving his identity. Key details about the crime were established through the witness, but his hesitation in answering certain questions raised issues.

During a subsequent court hearing in early February the next year, Mr. Pesukic was found guilty of manslaughter alongside drug offenses. Testimony from the witness was deemed reliable enough considering substantial threats to the witness's safety. Courts mentioned other witnesses' fear and ties to the accused. 

To balance defense rights, witness anonymity measures were justified. Although full background check details were withheld, these limitations were still deemed reasonable by the court. The case hinged primarily around the anonymous witness's account, corroborated by other pieces of evidence implicating the accused.
0.75.84:
The case began after a Turkish woman named Nurcan Güngil filed a complaint with the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), claiming that the Turkish government's handling led her to lose significant money through a brokerage firm. She filed an application on July 30, 2003.

Nurcan Güngil was born on 1958, resided in Ankara. In 1995, she entrusted about TRL1.5 million in Turkish liras towards purchasing Treasury bonds by Global A.Ş. However, the funds ended up being invested instead, in stocks, which devaluated significantly thereby causing her financial losses. 

In response to her inquiries in autumn, 1995, the broker personally confirmed having invested the money into the requested bonds. But in 1996, she discovered the broker had actually utilized these funds to purchase losing stocks instead of Treasury bonds. 

She initiated legal proceedings via the Ankara Commercial Court in September of that same year. On May 2017, the court partially awarded her, ordering the firm and the broker to repay her about 900 million Turkish liras along with simple interest, yet both parties contested.

In 2000, the Court of Cassation overturned that decision. Afterward, the case was reinstated into the Ankara Commercial Court, and in Nov. '21, they ruled again in her favor, requiring the defendant to repay her about 2500 million Turkish liras and interest. Despite the appeal by one side, by Oct '22, this ruling stood confirmed as final by similar higher judicial body.

Finally, in January 2023, she requested additional clarification which was denied by another court ruling in April '20.
0.75.85: The application originated through a case (number 3429/07), brought forth on the 20 July 2007 to the European Court under provisions stated in Articles of the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. 0.75.86:
The case stemmed from a complaint (number undisclosed, but filed in May, 2006 under the Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms against Turkish Republic) by Mr.Nuri Akalın, Turkish citizen. Ms İ. Kadirhan and Ms G. Tuncer were his legal representatives, working from Istanbul. The Turkish government was represented through their official delegate. In May of '09, the President of Second Section notified the government. Admissibility along side merits were also addressed (earlier Article 29 § 3). Details of the incident: Nuri Akalın was born in 1977. He was apprehended on suspicion of belonging an illegal organization in March, '97. A medical check revealed hyperaemia on his thighs. During interrogation, he claimed physical mistreatment while in custody, though didn't specify. A judge ordered his pre-trail confinement that same month. The State Security Court indicted him for attempted subversion of constitutional order, pursuant to former Criminal Code's Article '146' in April 1997. A statement about torture during police interrogation was made at the court in July of 1997 again but he provided no specifics there too.

In late-01, following conviction under the same charge, the Court of Cassation reversed that ruling. Post amendment to the laws on June, 04, abolishing security courts, the charges were heard by the Istanbul Assize Court. Between December 2008 and early 2009, he contested his ongoing detention twice unsuccessfully. The 11th Chamber dismissed both appeals, citing the nature, gravity and evidence related issues. No hearings took place.

The case concluded with conviction in April of the year 2009. As the case is still pending at the higher court, the lower court continued to review and decide on his continued detention after each hearing, considering factors such as the level of evidence and the circumstances involved, the potential danger of flight, the length and reasons behind detention so far, and the ongoing basis for keeping him in custody.
0.75.87:
The case began from an application filed before the European Court of Human Rights ("the Court") by Polish citizen, Marianna Cieślak against the Republic of Poland through an application number 32098/05. The case was filed using Article 34 of the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and was lodged August the tenth in twenty-five. For the case, the Polish government was represented by Mr Wołąsiewicz from their Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

On the twenty-seventh in the year of 2007, the president of Fourth Section of the Court sent the application's notice out. The Court, applying section two-nine three of convention, decided simultaneously to deal with admissibility of the case as much as its merit. 

Marianna Cieślak is a Polish national born 1923 whose current place of living is Bobolice.

A. With regards to the proceedings for expropriation, after her mother-in-law death on nineteenth seventy-five, during the proceedings for how to split inheritance, the Mayor of Warsaw’s Wola District on the thirty-first of October eighteen-eighty took part in expropriating the applicant's land. Her husband then inherited the plot of land in Warsaw on second February eighty-one and after his death on eighth August nineteen-eighty-eight, she became co-owner of the land.

Since then, she began proceedings for annulment of said expropriation decision. After the Supreme Administrative Court's decision approving that the expropriation was made against the law on the twenty-second of March ninety-one, the Warsaw Governor's Office quashed this decision on the twenty-ninth day of February nineteen-hundreds-six. The Polish Allotment Association appealed this decision and on the twentieth January nineteen-hundreds-eight, the Supreme Administrative Court confirmed the Warsaw Governor's Office’s opinion.

On third March nineteen-hundred-fifteen Marianna and others initiated a claim for repossession of the expropriated land with the Warsaw District Court. The case was transferred over to the Warsaw Regional Court which in the meanwhile gave a preliminary judgment on the nineteenth November two-thousand. The court ruled that the property would need to return and the parties hold the land until completion of financial claims. Marianna appealed after receiving a judgment. Later on eighteen January two-thousand-two the Warsaw Court of Appeal invalidated the Regional Court judgment on retaining possession till completion.

On the twenty-fifth day in the month of February two-thousand-four, the Regional Court passed an order stating the property should go to the applicant. Polish Allotment Association appealed the judgement and the Appeals Court rejected such appeal on twentieth December two-thousand and five. On sixth June two-thousand and six, it issued writ of execution.

B. Under 2004 Act, the applicant lodged a complaint before the Warsaw Court of Appeal on the twenty-second January 2005. The complaint was based upon the Act on complaints regarding the violation of rights for fair trial within a reasonable time (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki – "the 2004 Act"), enacted in June sixteenth in 2004 and effective since September seventeenth, two-thousand and four. Despite the fact that the Court of Appeal dismissed applicant's complaint in March the twenty-third in 2005. They concluded that there has no inactivity or excessive delay in proceedings after September 2004. Thus, no right to fair trial within the reasonable time was breached.
0.75.88: The case began after Poland's national citizen Mirosław Wroński filed a complaint in the European Court of Human Rights based upon the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. His case was heard alongside the Polish government. The applicant, who hails from the region around Gdynia in Poland where he resides, faced disciplinary action by the police force and criminal charges.
