There followed an appeal process and a dismissal of Mr Wroński’s complaints. Additionally, Wroński lodged his complaint under a specific law concerning delays and rights to a fair trial in late autumn '06, but this too was rejected by higher courts.
0.75.89:
The application came to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention, concerning Poland. Two citizens from Lublin, Poland—Mr Zdzisław Olesiński was from 1925 birthyear while Mrs Helena Olesińska, her birthyear unknown, brought a claim against the government. On the 21 of May, 1993 their neighbors received authorization from authorities permitting a retail business on one floor of his building. They contested the authority's decision, which was reaffirmed in July. In '94, the Olesińskis protested, stating a violation in city planning and a nuisance from the business. By early February in 1995, the authority rejected their challenge. However, by the 11 April that year, the town’s oversight board reversed its decision. Despite several communications between then and spring of two-thousand-sixteen about ongoing matters, the primary cause of delays was acquiring expert assessment, completed on four April nine-six.

The applicants continued to protest, leading to another denial by the ministry on April 1996. The applicants then appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, but the court ruled that the initial appeal should go through the Inspector first. The applicants did as instructed, and despite a decision in their favor, they still sought recourse with the Supreme Administrative Court, which on May 1st, 1998, denied their request. This stemmed from an application filed in July prior to that year, presented on behalf of two German nationals, Mrs Hildegard and Monika, who both faced allegations concerning violations under the terms of the European Convention of Human Rights. The case began on June 24, 2005 when a Polish citizen, Mr. Tomasz Kwiatkowski ("the applicant"), filed an application (no specific number cited in the original text but stated it is no 24254/05 in the original) through Article 34 of the Convention for Protecting Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case was referred to the Polish Government represented by Mr J. Wołąsiewicz and was related specifically with alleged unfairness of lustration process, violating the applicant's rights as described in Article 6. The Fourth Section's President delivered notification about the case on Oct 08 2008 to the Government.

On the 24th of April 1997 the Parliament approved a law requiring certain public officers like judges, prosecutors or lawyers to disclose any work or cooperation with the state's security services prior the year of 1990 during the communist period. This law took effect from August the 03 rd, 1997. By this law, Mr Kwiatkowski, an advocate, was asked about his involvement which led to a declared lack. In April of 2000, the Warsaw Court of Appeal received a request from the Public Interest Commissioner to start an investigation due to suspicion over his declaration. After the inquiry, the Warsaw Court of Appeal found the applicant's declaration false, although the rationale of decision was kept confidential, thus inaccessible for the applicant according to the criminal procedure code. The matter began following a complaint filed (case #48247/06) against Poland through article thirty-four of the European Convention on Human Rights on the eleventeenth of November, 2006 by Mr. Grzegorz Dublas who resides at Pruszcz Gdański. Mr.J. Wołąsiewicz representing his nation, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, was involved. Dublas claimed, amongst other issues, that his incarceration duration prior and during a criminal case exceeded what was justified by Article Three of Chapter Five and Article One of Chapter Six of the said convention.

On the eighteenth day of June in the year 2004; he faced apprehension by law enforcement officials. On the ninth day, June 9 of twenty-four, a local court in Gdansk determined there being sufficient cause to detain him pending further investigation due to suspicions of drug trafficking, along with a concern that he might flee. He remained incarcerated based primarily these factors and others including the necessity of thorough investigation. On September the second and again the fourth November of forty-four, the detention period was extended. Subsequently, on October twenty-six of the same year he received formal charges. His conditions of confinement continued to be reviewed and extended by the court.

Given that his initial two-year detention period as set in Article Three of Chapter Six hundred sixty-three of the Criminal Procedure Code was nearing its end, the court repeatedly asked a higher tribunal for permission past this limit for additional detention because of ongoing criminal investigations. This permission came through on the nineteenth May and the seventeenth August, 2006. The high court referenced the aforementioned concerns alongside estimated severe potential sentencing.

The first session of the trial took place one day after the new year in the year twenty-five. Regular intervals between sessions followed. The applicant's requests to be freed before this period ended alongside his appeals against the decisions extending his confinement were unsuccessful. On October seventeen in six, the high court extended his confinement until November twentieth six. They based both this and earlier extensions as necessary for conducting trials effectively and considering a potentially serious outcome of the case. He was released on the twentieth November thereafter since no further extension was approved for him.

In eight August of six, Dublas filed a grievance under the sixth segment of the legislation enacted in the seventeenth day, June 2004, concerning his right for a timely trial. In the third of November same year, the regional court in Gdansk dismissed Dublas’ complaint, asserting that his trial proceeded swiftly with no delays. At present time these proceedings are still pending in trial court.

The document details a case initiated on behalf of Mrs Waleria Kroenitz under the Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms in relation to Poland's actions. The case centered predominantly around delays during the legal process concerning her property restitution claims.

Mrs Kroenitz, a Polish citizen residing today at Przemyśl, saw her property taken by the state in 1948 and subsequently had the expropriation reversed via a minister's decision. She then sought to reclaim both her property and lost income from a company named Domgos through legal proceedings which began in Częstochowa. Despite multiple hearings, including those in early 2001 and later in 2002 where the expert testimony did not materialize due various reasons such as non-appearance, the legal court eventually ruled in favor, offering her compensation.

Additionally, she pursued similar claims for state compensation through the economic minister, who denied these initially. This prompted her to file suit in Warsaw and despite advancements at the regional level, ultimately lost when the appeals court upheld this decision on January 7, 2002.
The legal process was protracted over multiple years, with numerous setbacks, including the absence of key experts and adjournments, indicating significant delays in resolving the applicant’s claims for both restitution of her property rights and compensation for losses incurred over many years due the state’s actions prior to 1948.
The case was considered urgent within the European Court of Human Rights, highlighting the perceived breach of the "reasonable time" clause stipulated in the convention.

The case began when Polish citizen Mr. Artur Nowak, born on 1976, filed an application to the European Court of Human Rights on 17th of July in year 2002 through the "Convention of Human Rights." This application was made against Republic of Poland and was communicated about a complaint related with the duration taken while processing. Poland was represented throughout by their legal teams like Ms. S. Jaczewska from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and later Mr J. Wołasiwicz.

The story unfolds in December '93 where at seventeen years Artur, unfortunately faced a vehicular mishap caused by Mr. R. Z, a driver, leading to partial amputation in his left leg. In response to the incident, he pursued a civil lawsuit through Piotrków Regional Court against the State Insurance Company in June 1994 seeking compensation for both financial and emotional distress amounting to over eight hundred million old zlotys. The court waived court fees due to his young age.

The legal proceedings began on August the twelfth of '94, including an expert review and medical records inquiry. Following this, several other hearings took place intermittently during the years '95-98, witnessing more testimonies from experts, and Mr.Z joining the lawsuit as a party. Disappointingly, most critical stages of the proceedings were delayed or rescheduled due unforeseen circumstances such as cancellations because the advocate was ill or the applicant changed his claim.

On the twelfth month of '98, the Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court issued an initial judgment providing compensation along with a monthly stipend to Artur Nowak. Following this, a contesting appeal was submitted by Mr.R.Z. which was reviewed and modified by the Łódź Court of Appeal in early '99. In 2002, the Supreme Court of Poland had a review hearing and partially agreed on the appeal.

In summary, Mr.A.B, through legal processes, was awarded a sum of money for past damages and a continuous financial assistance but faced extensive delays in the proceedings.

The case began with a complaint brought against the Republic of Turkey in April 18, 2007 (Application Number no.17725/07). It was filed by Mr. Necmettin Alkan through his mother, Ms.L. Alkan under Article 34 of the European Convention for Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish government responded through a representative, while the applicant claimed that his right was violated by being denied legal aid, a right fundamentally linked with access into court.

The facts of Mr.Alkan's case revealed he was born in the year of 1979 and resided then (and now presumably) as an individual living in a town called Kars in Turkey.

In 2002 after finishing his mandatory armed service, he was declared mentally unfit under the care of his father named S.A. by a local judge known as the Sarıkamış Magistrates' Court. Following this, Mr.Alkan had a series of encounters with the military command over his health issues which stemmed from his military service. However these claims were dismissed following a medical examination from an institution known as the Gülhane Military Medical Academy. This medical report affirmed that his condition was likely due rather to factors beyond the military service.

Guarded under the watchful eye of the father as stipulated in the law due to mental health status, Mr. Alkan proceeded with seeking compensation from another high court, the Supreme Military Administrative Court, contending that his ailments were caused during his military tenure due to maltreatment. Providing proof of his prior good health through multiple medical assessments taken before joining services, he formally submitted for legal aid assistance to cover court fees, accompanied by documentation attested by the village headman about the family's financial constraints.

Despite these efforts, the application for legal aid was turned down twice by the aforementioned court in July (19th) of that year and again in November. They cited the lack of adequate evidence supporting his case and absence in proving he lacked funds to pay the court's required fee.

On November the same year, the court notified the applicant to remit a sum amounting to approximately 1,400 euros within three weeks. As per the official record, payment was not forthcoming and consequently, the claims for compensation were subsequently abandoned on 10 January of one thousand eight hundred seven (2007).

The case began following Mr Tadeusz Cegielski's application, filed pursuant to Article 34 of the Convention for Protection of Human Rights in early 2000, against his native Poland regarding a protracted legal dispute. On January 19, 2003, the Court communicated the concern around long proceedings and perceived ineffective remedies to Poland. According to the Court’s procedures outlined under Article 29, it simultaneously assessed the application and its validity.

Mr. Tadeusz Cegielski was born in 1933 and resided in Bielsko-Biała. In March of 1993, the Szczecin Regional Court overturned an earlier 1947 verdict from a Military Court that had incarcerated Tadeusz’s father along with confiscating his property.

In 1995, Tadeusz obtained a compensation award for his father's incarceration from the Szczecin Regional Court's Criminal Chamber. In late September 1995 he commenced civil litigation with the State Treasury for damages related to his father’s estate and machinery.

In January of ’96, the trial court sought access to the case documentation from a Criminal Chamber of the same court where Tadeusz’s application was initially handled; they received these documents later in the year.

The first hearing took place in early '99, where Tadeusz testified and the court planned to hear testimonies from three witnesses scheduled in Mysliborz District Court.

Between '99 to '00, several hearings occurred, including an application for partial judgment on loss-income claims and the addition of new parties like ministers of finance and treasury. Expert opinions on property valuation from both machinery and land were sought during this period.

On October 20, '00, the court issued partial compensation of PLN 211,105; however, the total compensation was not finalized. In response, the Minister of Treasury appealed the decision, but the Poznan Court of Appeal retained the original ruling. The Supreme Court is currently deliberating an appeal by Treasury. Meanwhile, the outstanding claims remain pending at the trial court.

The case began on 17 June, 2005. It was brought forward on behalf of a Polish citizen named Jarosław Kyzioł against his homeland - Poland by the European Court of Human Rights. The Polish authorities, represented by Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, took part through diplomacy and legal representation.

The case was initiated in accordance to article three-fourth of the European Convention for the protection against human rights and fundamental freedoms. The European Court of Human Rights decided in December the year 2006, that the application would be noticed to Poland.

The Court ruled on both the admissibility along the merits of this case simultaneously, using article twenty-nine section three of convention. 

Jarosław Kyzioł was born during 1969 in Cracow, Poland and still resides in the city. He is part of multiple land co-ownerships. In October 1994 a housing cooperative submitted a request for the dissolution of co-ownership for five plots of land he claimed to share. At first, there 182 parties involved in said proceedings, a number expanded to 417 later due to additional parties.

In 1997, the Cracow Regional Court joined a case that involved claims to the same land. The same year, an expert was assigned by the district court to work in geodesy. His findings became evidence on 19 July of that year; however, on the next year, the court asked another expert report to update initial one, delivered late June 03. In November 2003 and December of the same years, decisions were made to exclude certain judges from the proceedings. Also in mid-December of fiscal year 2004, the court paused proceedings because of recent deaths. The proceedings were resumed in spring 06 due to legal heirs joining in. But again, the court decided to halt the proceedings on account of further deaths among the parties. 

In 15 December the same year 2005, Kyzioł lodged another complaint related with the unreasonable duration of the case. On 3rd month of following year the Cracow Regional Court dismissed said complaint. The court noted that the law mentioned on the complaint was effective after 04th September 04 and therefore the complaint would be assessed only based events after that date. The court also mentioned that the pause in the case was because of delays by the legal heirs in submitting documents and the large number of evolving parties.

Çakıroğlu, a practicing lawyer from the area, and Mr Servet Durdu based out of Ankara born the following year, 1965; he had legal support through M. Bayat, also a practicing lawyer from the same city—lodged applications against Turkey, referred via Article 34 of the Convention for protecting human rights (the Convention). The cases were marked under application numbers nos., 27080/08 and another 40982/08. The presidential authority of Second Section issued notification to the state as represented by their agent on an assigned date, May thirtieth in 2009, along with deciding to review the applications both for admissibility as well as merits simultaneously per Article 29, section 2.

Regarding the details of the cases, they involved two parties each. For Mr. Metin Köksal in case nos. 27080/08, he had previously been released from active service due a criminal conviction established by a martial court ruling in 2001. His conviction had been finalized by late 2001. In early 2002, Köksal contested this via the Samsun Administrative Court to invalidate his dismissal. However, his request was denied by this court on June fifth. By 2005, the highest administrative tribunal reaffirmed Samsun's ruling. Public prosecutor and the judge rapporteur's opinions were not conveyed, the final denial being reached by December 2007.

For Mr Servet Durdu's case nos., 40982/08, similar procedural actions were initiated when he was dismissed from his official duties in early March, 2002, following disciplinary proceedings tied up to the same grounds. After being acquitted by the Ankara Assize Court in June of the same year and having his acquittal confirmed later by the Court of Appeals, the administrative court yet again determined that even though he was found not guilty of the criminal charges, his civil service termination still stood valid according to specific provisions outlined within the Civil Servants' Law. The applicant's appeal to annul the decision made in 2004 by the Administrative Court was upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court on a subsequent date, March twenty-sixth, 2005—the opinions from the prosecutor and judge rapporteur did not reach him. In the end, the Supreme Administrative Court in January, 2008, declined his effort to correct its ruling. The notification of these decisions was received in early spring, March the 4th, of 2008.

alpha_beta_0.01.2: The case began with an application from a Turkish national to the European Court of Human Rights alleging that he did not receive legal assistance during his period of police custody. The lawyer representing the individual was practicing in Gaziantep. The government was represented by an agent. On a certain date, the court declared the case partially inadmissible and communicated the issue of insufficient legal assistance to the applicant during police custody to the government. The court also examined the case's merits alongside its admissibility. The applicant, who was born in a specific year and currently serves a prison term, was arrested during a military operation in 2007 on suspicion of being a member of an illegal armed organization. He was detained at a gendarme station without legal representation, and a detailed statement was recorded. The statement mentioned the applicant joined a certain group in 2005 and committed various acts of violence. On the same day, he appeared before a prosecutor and subsequently an investigating judge, where he confirmed the verbatim statement. The applicant was detained on remand the same day. A prosecutor filed an indictment on December 6, 2007, charging the applicant with attempting to secede part of the country's territory and seeking the death penalty under the Criminal Code. The trial started on May 21, 2008, before a jury, with the applicant represented by his lawyer. He admitted to joining the group and receiving training but claimed his statement was falsified. On May 17, 2008, the jury found him guilty and sentenced him to death. The sentence was later changed. The court confirmed the applicant's involvement in illegal activities and killings of village guards based on evidence presented during the trial and his statement during arrest. The applicant's appeal was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on a specific date.
alpha_beta_0.01.3: The case originated with two applications against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights by two Turkish nationals, referred to as Applicants A and B, pertaining to a complaint under the former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants, who received legal aid, were represented by a lawyer from Istanbul. The Turkish Government did not appoint a representative for the proceedings. The First Section of the Court decided to combine the applications, declare some as inadmissible, and inform the Government about the complaints under Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 and Article 8 of the Convention. Later, the Court changed its composition twice. The case was assigned to the newly formed Section. The applicants and the Government submitted responses to each other regarding the merits of the case. The Court decided to handle admissibility and the merits together. The applicants, referred to as A and B, were arrested by security police in Ankara in connection with an illegal organization investigation. They were detained in police custody from 11:45 p.m. on the date of arrest until 11:45 p.m. the next day, under an extension authorized by the prosecutor. They were interrogated by the prosecutor the same day but were not brought before a judge until the following morning. They were released on provisional bail for A and remanded for B. The prosecutor indicted them and they were charged with aiding and abetting an armed gang under Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code. After a trial, A was released while B remained in custody. B was found guilty and sentenced to a term of imprisonment and a ban on public office for three years. Upon appeal, the Court of Cassation overturned the conviction due to misclassification of the offense. The case was deferred for a decision.
alpha_beta_0.01.4:
The case began as an application against the Republic of Poland by a Polish national on 15 July 2015. The case was brought under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Government were represented by an agent of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant claimed that his placement in the "dangerous detainee" regime and its extended application constituted inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3 of the Convention. On 25 July 2015, the complaint was communicated to the Government. The remaining parts of the application were declared inadmissible according to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

The facts of the case followed. The applicant was born in 1975 and is currently detained. He was initially arrested and remanded in custody on 15 July 2015. He was suspected of murder and inciting murder against a witness who intended to testify against him. He was convicted of murder on 10 June 2016. The classification of the applicant as a "dangerous detainee" was made by the "dangerous detainee" commission. The commission placed the applicant in a designated wing or cell for increased security. The applicant did not appeal. This classification was upheld multiple times, with the period of the regime extended over more than ten years. The justification for extending the regime was his serious charges and poor moral character. The applicant appealed against the last decision, but the Warsaw Regional Court dismissed it as lawful. The dangerous detainee regime for the applicant was lifted on 12 January 2021.

The applicant was housed in a monitored cell, with naked body searches conducted every time he entered or left the cell.
alpha_beta_0.01.5:
The case began when a Turkish national submitted an application to the European Commission of Human Rights regarding an alleged violation of their human rights. This application, which did not specify a case number, was filed under the obsolete Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The individual was legally represented by a lawyer based in Ankara. The Turkish Government did not appoint an official to represent their interests during the proceedings before the Convention institutions. In a decision rendered on an unspecified date, the Court of Human Rights partially rejected the application and communicated a complaint about the fairness of the proceedings to the Turkish government. Simultaneously, it decided to examine both the admissibility and the merits of the application. 

The case facts chronicled that the individual was born and resided in Turkey. On an unspecified date, they were taken into custody by police officers from the Antalya Security Directorate on suspicion of associating with an unnamed illegal organization. The applicant was later taken to the Antalya Security Directorate for questioning where they signed a document. The candidate claimed they were coerced and mistreated during the signing process. On an unspecified date, a judge ordered their detention. On another unspecified date, the public prosecutor of the Izmir State Security Court submitted an indictment against the applicant, alleging criminal activity under Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to a determined period of imprisonment on an unspecified date. Additionally, the court prohibited them from working in the government. The court of cassation upheld the decision on yet another unspecified date, pronouncing the verdict in their absence without notifying them. On a further unspecified date, the judgment of the court of cassation was deposited with the Izmir State Security Court. The applicant's representative informed the Court on an unspecified date that they were conditionally released from prison after serving three-quarters of their sentence.
alpha_beta_0.01.6:
The case started with an application against the Republic of Poland, made under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights by a Polish citizen, on an unspecified date. The Polish Government responded to the case through their representative from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court communicated about the possible interception of the applicant's correspondence. The Court decided to look into the complaint about interception and consider the admissibility of the case at the same time. 

In the factual background, the applicant is described as a Polish national who has been involved in criminal proceedings for drug trafficking. He was initially detained and then sentenced to a specific period of imprisonment, with the exact dates and duration not provided. The applicant appealed the initial judgment, and the final appeal confirmed his conviction with a different sentence.

The document also mentions several instances where the applicant's letters to the Court were reportedly intercepted. It talks about stamps indicating censorship, along with handwritten dates and illegible signatures. Additional letters were cut open, resealed with tape, and sometimes part of the envelope was missing. The applicant complained to the Court about the censorship of his mail.

Following these complaints, the applicant received a letter from the President of the Polish Office informing him that his letters were not censored and the previous stamps were merely mistakes.
alpha_beta_0.01.7: The case began with an application by Polish citizens in the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants, including the first and third applicants and the second applicant, filed a lawsuit against a company in a Polish court on a specific date. A judgment was issued by a court, and both parties appealed. The Supreme Court overturned the initial judgment and sent the case back to a lower court. An expert provided an opinion, and multiple hearings were held over several dates. The lower court issued a judgment, which was also appealed. The appeal court amended this judgment and ordered a larger compensation to the applicants. The applicants then appealed to the Supreme Court, which dismissed their appeal without making changes. On a certain date, the Supreme Court ordered the applicants to pay cassation fees based on the defendant's lawyer's request.
alpha_beta_0.01.8: The application originated from an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by several individuals who were members of the executive and auditing boards of a non-governmental organization. Officers from the governor's office and the Ankara Security Directorate inspected the organization’s headquarters and discovered violations of certain laws, which led to fines being imposed on the members of the boards and a bill of indictment being filed against them by the public prosecutor. When the accused failed to pay the fines within the stipulated time, the Ankara Magistrates' Court sentenced them to a higher fine. The applicants further maintained that they were not given a fair trial because they could not present their defenses, but this was dismissed by the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance.
alpha_beta_0.01.9: The case began as an application against the Republic of Turkey by a Turkish national. The applicant, whose exact details are not provided, was represented by unnamed lawyers. The Turkish Government were defended by their legal agent. The complaint relating to alleged interference with the applicant's right to freedom of expression and assembly was communicated to the Government on a specific date, while the remainder of the application was deemed inadmissible. The facts of the case involved the applicant, who was born and resides in Turkey, and holds a specific position in a political party. The party held its first ordinary congress at a restaurant in Ankara, where the applicant was elected as the meeting's chairman. A public prosecutor filed an indictment against the party, including the applicant, due to alleged violations of Law No. 2820. The applicant acknowledged speaking from the chair but argued his actions were within his constitutional rights as a member of the political party. He further stated that all speeches in question were in the delegates' native languages, rendering them legal and ethical. The Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance convicted the applicant on the grounds of not stopping delegates from speaking in their native language despite warnings. However, the application for the case to be transferred to the Constitutional Court to review the legality of Law No. 2820 was denied. The Court of Cassation overturned the first-instance judgment because the court had not examined whether the suspension conditions of Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were met. Ultimately, the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance terminated the proceedings due to the expiration of the statutory time limit.

The case originated in an application against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. A Turkish national brought the case. The individual was represented by a lawyer from Bursa. The Turkish Government was represented by their Agent. The President of the Second Section decided to notify the Government of the application. The Court decided to assess the admissibility and merits of the application simultaneously. 

The applicant, who was born in an unspecified year and lives in Bursa, had his plot of land seized by the General Directorate of Highways without formal expropriation for the construction of a highway in a unspecified year. The applicant sought compensation through a legal action, requesting 5,500 Turkish liras and reserving the right to increase the claim later. The primary court awarded 5,500 Turkish liras plus interest. Execution proceedings were initiated to obtain the award amount. The Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance judgment. 

Subsequently, the applicant filed an additional action based on a higher expert report valuation, requesting additional compensation. The court of appeal awarded further compensation plus interest. New execution proceedings were initiated to recoup this award.

The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the court of appeal. The state paid the first award to the execution file before the Bursa Execution Office. They later paid the additional award to another execution file. According to the applicant, there is no outstanding debt in the execution files.

The applicant, represented by a lawyer named from Nicosia and granted legal aid, alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived her of her home and properties. The case was transmitted to the Court on November 1, 1998, following the application of Protocol No. 11 to the European Convention on Human Rights, and was declared admissible by the Court in an unspecified decision. The applicant and the Government provided observations on the merits, and the Government of Cyprus exercised its right to intervene.

The applicant, born in an unspecified year, lived in Nicosia. She resided in a village called the village, situated in the district, before the Turkish military evicted her and her family in 1974. The applicant claimed ownership of two houses in the village, built in 1916 and 1958 respectively. The first house was ancestral, a spacious two-story home with marble floors and a titled roof, and the second was a seaside holiday home with two bedrooms. She provided several documents with the Department of Lands and Surveys of the Republic of Cyprus, asserting her legal and registered ownership of these properties. The applicant claimed she was prevented from returning to her home and properties due to continuous occupation by Turkish military authorities.

In 1974, the applicant attempted to return to her home and properties by participating in a convoy of fellow refugees. The organizers informed the Commander of the United Nations forces in Cyprus of their intention. At the checkpoint between Nicosia and Famagusta, the applicant and refugees requested permission from a UN officer to return. The UN officer informed them that their request had been denied by the Turkish military authorities.

The case originated from an application against the Republic of Turkey by a Turkish national, represented by a lawyer from Izmir. The application, initially lodged under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, was declared partly inadmissible by the Court on a specific date. The communications included the lack of legal assistance during police custody and non-communication of the Principal Public Prosecutor's submissions. The Court examined admissibility and merits simultaneously pursuant to Article 29 § 3.

The applicant, born in a particular year and residing in Izmir, was arrested by anti-terrorism branch officers of the Izmir Security Directorate on suspicion of participating in an illegal demonstration for the support of an imprisoned leader. Additionally, he was accused of hanging an illegal placard on a bridge in the city on a certain date. He provided a statement to the police admitting these charges on a specific day, but later denied them to the public prosecutor and investigating judge, claiming coercion. On the same day, the investigating judge ordered the applicant's continued custody. 

The public prosecutor at the Izmir State Security Court submitted an indictment in the same court on another date, accusing the applicant of aiding and abetting an offense under Article 169 of the Criminal Code and Section 5 of Law No. 3713 (anti-terrorism law). The applicant was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment, which was later reduced. The case began with an application in 2011 against the Kingdom of Denmark by a Danish national, John Dancer, through lawyer Lars Drager. The Danish Government was represented by Aldis Allsektor of the Ministry for Justice. In late 2011, the Fifth Section decided to inform the Government and rule on admissibility and merits concurrently. 

In the late 1990s, Denmark introduced a phenomenon known as "reorganisation". It was defined as criminal activity occurring when individuals involved in stripping companies of their assets committed financial grievances for profit, often rumored to happen through professional collusion and within short periods. 

By the end of 1996, it was estimated that close to one thousand six hundred enterprises were stripped, involving extensive tax debts. Following this, numerous legal controversies arose among various sellers' and buyers' banks regarding liability for losses brought about by their involvement in these stripping incidents. Through legislative adjustments, such practices largely ceased by 1998. 

On February 20, 2008, John Dancer sold a company originally known as Topco Ltd but renamed Merco Ltd. On 20 May 2010, Merco Ltd declared bankruptcy, and a trustee managed its assets. On 25 August 2010, the trustee sued Dancer and a bank, Kommerzbank, for losses. Dancer later sued his advisers, the accounting firm Top Accounts, and lawyers Best Law for misleading him. The case was ongoing and involved several legal engagements and communications between parties until the Supreme Court judgment in a related case. The progress of the case was also marked by multiple adjournments and the appointment of new counsel. Court proceedings concluded on 3 March 2015, finding against Dancer. On 16 April 2015, Dancer appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court.

Specifically, she argued that the same judge who had adjudicated the second-instance judgment and who had decided the appeal's inadmissibility, rendered the proceedings unfair. Dismissing her appeal, the Supreme Court referenced its prior rulings highlighting that a failing to enumerate circumstances justifying the cassation appeal's examination is serious and irreparable. The Court also noted that this requirement ties into its established grounds for refusing cassation appeals. In response to the applicant's objection, the Supreme Court reasoned that the participation of the judge in both stages of the proceedings was not relevant.

The Warsaw Governor's Office quashed the Mayor's decision and dismissed an expropriation application filed by an unnamed party on 28 April 2007. The applicant appealed this preliminary judgment, and the Warsaw Court of Appeal ruled on 15 August 2007. The Court of Appeal reversed the Regional Court's ruling on the right to retain possession until completing financial claims on 15 September 2007. On 15 October 2007, the Regional Court issued a definitive decision to return the property. The applicant and the expropriating party both appealed, and the Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 15 November 2007, issuing a writ of enforcement on the same day.

Additionally, the applicant filed a complaint under the June 2004 Act regarding a breach of the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time to the Warsaw Court of Appeal on 15 December 2007. The Court of Appeal dismissed the complaint, noting that as of its entry into force on 1 January 2006, there had been no inactivity in proceedings and therefore no breach of the right to a fair trial.
